title: Episode 280: Babe Ruth: The Sultan of Swat, the Called Shot, and the House That Ruth Built
description:
The larger-than-life, joyous, and mythic story of George Herman 'Babe' Ruth: the reform-school boy from the Baltimore waterfront who became the greatest and most iconic sports figure in American history. Beginning his career as a dominant World Series championship left-handed pitcher for the Boston Red Sox, Ruth's unprecedented home run power revolutionized baseball from a low-scoring game of bunts and steals into a thrilling spectacle of towering blasts. Sold to the New York Yankees in 1919 for cash to finance a Broadway play, Ruth single-handedly saved baseball following the 1919 Black Sox scandal, hitting sixty home runs in 1927 and leading the legendary 'Murderers' Row'. Discover the Sultan of Swat.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series celebrates the roaring, irrepressible giant of the 1920s whose towering home runs and boundless appetite for life defined the golden age of American sports. Here is George with the legendary life of Babe Ruth.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE WATERFRONT URCHIN OF ST. MARY'S: 1895 TO 1914
Born in February 1895 above his grandfather's saloon in Baltimore, Maryland, George Herman Ruth Jr. was one of eight children born to German-American saloonkeeper George Sr. and Kate Schamberger, though only George and his sister Mamie survived infancy. Roaming the rough waterfront docks of Baltimore, skipping school, chewing tobacco, and stealing fruit from market carts, seven-year-old George was deemed 'incorrigible' by his overwhelmed parents, who committed him to St. Mary's Industrial School for Boys—a Catholic reformatory and orphanage run by the Xaverian Brothers. For twelve formative years, St. Mary's was young George's entire world. There, a towering six-foot-six monk named Brother Matthias Boutlier noticed the boy's astonishing physical strength and spent hours hitting fungoes to him on the dirt fields. Matthias became George's surrogate father, teaching him tailoring, personal discipline, and the fundamentals of pitching and hitting with a forty-ounce ash bat.  The waterfront slums of Baltimore in the late nineteenth century were rough, perilous breeding grounds for street gangs, where young George scavenged oysters from wooden sailing schooners and drank leftover beer from barroom dregs. The Xaverian Brothers at St. Mary's provided the unruly boy with the only structured sanctuary and moral love he had ever known, clothing him in blue denim uniforms and teaching him the patient trade of tailoring shirt collars. Brother Matthias Boutlier, a gentle giant who stood six feet six inches and weighed two hundred and fifty pounds, recognized that young George's wild energy could be channeled into athletic greatness, spending hours on the gravel diamond hitting grounders and teaching him to unleash his full torso into every swing.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE RED SOX PITCHING PHENOM: 1914 TO 1919
In 1914, Jack Dunn, owner of the minor league Baltimore Orioles, signed the nineteen-year-old phenom to his first professional contract, becoming his legal guardian. When Orioles players teased the wide-eyed newcomer as 'Jack Dunn's newest babe', the nickname stuck for eternity: Babe Ruth. Sold that summer to the Boston Red Sox, Ruth quickly emerged as the most dominant left-handed pitcher in the American League. From 1915 to 1918, Ruth won eighty-nine games, posted an exceptional 2.19 earned run average, and threw twenty-nine and two-thirds consecutive scoreless innings across two World Series—a pitching record that stood unbroken for forty-three years. But Ruth's hitting was so explosive that Red Sox manager Ed Barrow was forced to transition his ace pitcher into an everyday outfielder. In 1919, Ruth shattered the single-season home run record by blasting twenty-nine home runs, an unheard-of total at a time when entire teams rarely hit twenty home runs in a season.  Ruth's arrival in Boston established him as the premier southpaw hurler in the American League, compiling twenty-three wins in 1916 while leading the league with nine shutouts and an astonishing 1.75 earned run average. In the 1916 World Series against the Brooklyn Superbas, Ruth pitched a fourteen-inning complete-game masterpiece, allowing only one run and holding the National League champions hitless for eleven consecutive innings. His conversion to an everyday outfielder in 1919 produced the most explosive offensive explosion in baseball history: Ruth hit home runs of unprecedented distance that sailed over the roofs of stadium grandstands, prompting opposing teams to erect taller fences and forcing baseball manufacturers to switch to a livelier, cork-centered ball.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE CURSE OF THE BAMBINO AND THE 1920 NEW YORK RENAISSANCE
In December 1919, Red Sox owner Harry Frazee, cash-strapped and seeking capital to finance a Broadway musical titled 'No, No, Nanette', committed the most infamous transaction in sports history: he sold Babe Ruth to the New York Yankees for one hundred thousand dollars in cash and a three-hundred-thousand-dollar mortgage on Fenway Park. The transaction cursed the Red Sox to an eighty-six-year championship drought while igniting the greatest dynasty in American sports. Arriving in New York just as the 1919 Black Sox betting scandal threatened to destroy public trust in baseball, Ruth single-handedly revived the national pastime with sheer offensive fury. In 1920, his first year in pinstripes, Ruth smashed fifty-four home runs—out-hitting every single American League team combined except the Philadelphia Athletics. Batting averages soared, fans flooded the Polo Grounds in unprecedented multitudes, and Ruth became the undisputed king of New York.  The sale of Ruth to the Yankees transformed New York into the capital of American sporting culture, arriving at the exact moment that American society was emerging from the trauma of World War One and the Spanish Flu pandemic into the roaring prosperity of the 1920s. Before Ruth, baseball was dominated by the 'inside game' of sacrifice bunts, hit-and-run plays, and defensive pitching duels; Ruth single-handedly rendered that style obsolete by demonstrating that a single towering home run was worth three singles and a sacrifice. In his first season in New York, Ruth scored one hundred and fifty-eight runs, walked one hundred and fifty times, and recorded an unbelievable .847 slugging percentage that stood as a major league record for over eighty years.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE HOUSE THAT RUTH BUILT AND MURDERERS' ROW: 1923 TO 1927
The massive crowds flocking to see Ruth outgrew the Polo Grounds, prompting the Yankees to construct baseball's first three-tiered concrete-and-steel cathedral in the Bronx. Opening on April 18, 1923, before seventy-four thousand cheering spectators, Yankee Stadium was forever christened 'The House That Ruth Built'—a fitting tribute consummated when Ruth blasted a game-winning three-run home run against his former Boston teammates on Opening Day. In 1927, Ruth anchored the immortal 'Murderers' Row' lineup alongside Lou Gehrig, Earle Combs, and Tony Lazzeri. That season, Ruth achieved the mythical zenith of baseball immortality: on September 30, 1927, facing Tom Zachary of the Washington Senators, Ruth walloped his sixtieth home run into the right-field bleachers, a towering record that stood unchallenged for thirty-four years.  The construction of Yankee Stadium was a monumental architectural gamble: seating over sixty-two thousand fans, it was the largest sports arena in the Western hemisphere, featuring short right-field dimensions specifically tailored to Ruth's pull-hitting left-handed swing. The 1927 Yankees are widely considered the greatest baseball team ever assembled, winning one hundred and ten games and outscoring opponents by nearly four hundred runs. The friendly home-run race between Ruth and his quiet, scholarly teammate Lou Gehrig captivated the nation through the summer of 1927, culminating in Ruth's dramatic late-September surge where he blasted seventeen home runs in the final month to secure his immortal milestone of sixty home runs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE CALLED SHOT OF WRIGLEY FIELD: OCTOBER 1, 1932
During Game 3 of the 1932 World Series at Chicago's Wrigley Field, Ruth etched his name into American folklore with baseball's most famous moment. Facing intense razzing from the Chicago Cubs dugout and fans hurling lemons and insults, thirty-seven-year-old Ruth stepped into the batter's box against pitcher Charlie Root in the fifth inning. With two strikes against him, amid deafening boos, Ruth stepped out of the box, pointed his finger toward the deep center-field bleachers, and dug back in. On the next pitch, Ruth unleashed his magnificent, full-body uppercut swing, driving Root's fastball an estimated four hundred and ninety feet into the temporary center-field seats for the most dramatic home run in World Series history. Whether he pointed directly at the flagpole or merely signaled two strikes, the 'Called Shot' cemented Babe Ruth as an American demigod who could bend reality to his majestic will.  The hostility directed at Ruth during the 1932 World Series was fueled by the bitter dispute over former Cubs manager Joe McCarthy, whom the Yankees had hired to lead their pennant-winning squad. Cubs players stood along their dugout railing waving white towels and screaming that Ruth was washed up and overweight, while fans hurled fruit and rolled-up programs at him as he stepped to the plate. Ruth's gesture toward center field with two strikes was a moment of supreme theatrical defiance: driving Charlie Root's pitch over the deep center-field wire barrier into the temporary temporary wooden bleachers, Ruth trotted around the bases laughing and waving his cap to the stunned Chicago crowd in an unmatched display of athletic bravado.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE COLOSSUS OF APPETITE AND GENEROSITY
Off the diamond, Ruth lived with an unbridled, joyous hedonism that matched the roaring excess of the 1920s. He drove high-powered luxury roadsters at breakneck speeds, smoked twelve-inch Havana cigars, and consumed gargantuan feasts of six hot dogs, two porterhouse steaks, and quarts of ginger ale in a single sitting. When told that his eighty-thousand-dollar salary in 1930 exceeded that of President Herbert Hoover, Ruth famously quipped: 'I know, but I had a better year than he did!' Yet underneath his boisterous exterior beat a heart of pure, childlike generosity. Remembering his own lonely childhood at St. Mary's, Ruth spent hours visiting pediatric hospitals, orphanages, and polio wards without press fanfare, signing thousands of baseballs for sick children and famously promising a dying boy named Johnny Sylvester that he would hit a home run for him in the World Series—and then hitting three.  Ruth's immense celebrity made him the first modern American athlete to earn millions through commercial endorsements, appearing in national advertisements for clothing, candy bars, automobiles, and sporting goods under the shrewd management of Christy Walsh. His extravagant lifestyle was legendary: he bought fleets of custom Cadillacs, gave away hundred-dollar bills to shoeshine boys, and tip hotel bellhops with gold coins, embodying the lavish, uninhibited spirit of Jazz Age New York. His visits to hospital sickbeds were completely unscripted and heartfelt: he would sit beside crippled children, hold their hands, and tell funny stories about his childhood, displaying an instinctive empathy for the forgotten and downtrodden that endeared him to working-class Americans.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FINAL FAREWELL AT THE STADIUM: JUNE 1948 AND LEGACY
Ruth retired in 1935 with seven hundred and fourteen career home runs, a staggering 2,213 runs batted in, and an all-time record slugging percentage of .690 that has never been surpassed. In 1936, he was elected as one of the inaugural five members of the National Baseball Hall of Fame. In his final years, battling agonizing throat cancer, Ruth made his final, poignant appearance at Yankee Stadium on June 13, 1948, for the stadium's twenty-fifth anniversary. Leaning heavily on a baseball bat for support, his famous Number 3 retired on his back, Ruth gazed out at fifty thousand cheering fans through weeping eyes as photographer Nat Fein captured the Pulitzer Prize-winning photograph of his bowed silhouette. Passing away two months later at age fifty-three, over one hundred thousand mourners filed past his open casket at Yankee Stadium. Babe Ruth was more than a baseball player; he was the buoyant, roaring heartbeat of American optimism, proving that an abandoned boy from the streets could become the king of the world.  In his final years, Ruth longed to manage a Major League baseball team, but baseball owners feared his reckless personal habits and boisterous independence, shutting him out of front-office leadership. When he walked onto the diamond at Yankee Stadium for the final time in June 1948, his frail body ravaged by inoperable nasopharyngeal carcinoma, fifty thousand fans stood in weeping silence to honor the man who had brought them so much joy. Babe Ruth's seven hundred and fourteen home runs stood as an unassailable mountain of achievement for forty years, but his true immortality resides in the joyous, roaring spirit he breathed into American baseball, turning a simple summer game into an enduring cathedral of American dreams.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Babe Ruth's towering home runs, childlike joy, and iconic presence embodied the roaring spirit of twentieth-century America. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with the revolutionary musical life of Louis Armstrong, Satchmo, the founding father of American jazz. Until then, stay curious.
